reference.source: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases / WHO guidance
clinicalPearls: Caused by Old World hantaviruses (Hantaan, Seoul, Dobrava, and the milder Puumala causing nephropathia epidemica) acquired by inhaling aerosolised rodent excreta across Europe and Asia
The classic course progresses through febrile, hypotensive, oliguric, diuretic, and convalescent phases, though milder Puumala infection may not show all stages

Capillary leak drives retroperitoneal and renal interstitial oedema, and acute kidney injury with proteinuria and haematuria is the hallmark, distinguishing it from the pulmonary-predominant New World disease
Thrombocytopenia, elevated haematocrit from plasma leak, and haemorrhagic manifestations such as conjunctival haemorrhage and petechiae are common
Sudden severe lumbar and abdominal pain with blurred or transient myopia is a characteristic clue in Puumala infection
Management is supportive with careful fluid and electrolyte balance and renal replacement therapy when needed; some authorities have used ribavirin for severe early Hantaan disease
Diagnosis is confirmed by hantavirus serology and RT-PCR, interpreted alongside a rodent-exposure history in an endemic area
reference.pathophysiology: Inhaled virus from persistently infected rodent reservoirs infects vascular endothelium, and an immune-mediated increase in vascular permeability produces plasma leakage. In contrast to the pulmonary tropism of New World strains, Old World hantaviruses preferentially injure the renal microvasculature and interstitium, causing acute kidney injury with oliguria followed by a polyuric recovery phase. Platelet consumption and endothelial dysfunction underlie the bleeding tendency, and severity ranges from mild (Puumala) to severe (Hantaan and Dobrava).
additionalDifferentials: Acute glomerulonephritis or other causes of acute kidney injury
Other viral haemorrhagic fevers depending on geography
Thrombotic microangiopathy (haemolytic uraemic syndrome or thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura)
additionalInvestigations: Hantavirus serology for IgM and IgG antibodies
RT-PCR for viral RNA during the early febrile phase
Renal function tests, urinalysis, and quantification of proteinuria and haematuria
Full blood count monitoring platelets and haematocrit
Coagulation studies to assess for disseminated intravascular coagulation
Ultrasound of the kidneys showing enlarged, oedematous kidneys in nephropathia epidemica
redFlags: Progression to anuria or hyperkalaemia requiring urgent renal replacement therapy
Shock during the hypotensive phase from capillary leak
Overhydration precipitating pulmonary oedema during the oliguric phase
Neurological deterioration suggesting central nervous system involvement or severe electrolyte disturbance
reference.prognosis: Puumala-associated nephropathia epidemica is usually self-limiting with full renal recovery, whereas Hantaan and Dobrava infections carry appreciable mortality and greater risk of severe acute kidney injury; most survivors recover normal renal function.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis in the febrile phase before renal features appear
Aggressive fluid loading during the oliguric phase, precipitating volume overload
Attributing acute kidney injury solely to sepsis or nephrotoxins without considering hantavirus exposure
Underestimating the transition to the diuretic phase, risking hypovolaemia and electrolyte loss
Overlooking the rodent-exposure or rural travel history
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
World Health Organization guidance on haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome
management: Provide meticulous supportive care with phase-specific fluid and electrolyte management, restricting fluids during the oliguric phase and replacing losses during the polyuric phase
Consider ribavirin in severe, early Hantaan or Dobrava infection, recognising its uncertain benefit
Institute renal replacement therapy for oliguric acute kidney injury, fluid overload, or refractory electrolyte disturbance
Manage haemorrhagic complications and disseminated intravascular coagulation with blood-product support, and avoid nephrotoxic drugs
Monitor renal function, platelet count, haematocrit, blood pressure, and urine output closely through the disease phases
Refer to infectious diseases and nephrology, and advise rodent-exposure avoidance and control for prevention
